doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Songs from the 1980s and 1990s, including Was
summary: Amy and Audre name favorites, such as Was, Numbers on Paper and Ever Since the World Ended.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: And you kept writing songs through the ‘80s and ‘90s.
No. I don’t write songs any more.
But in the ‘80s and ‘90s.
Oh yeah. Well, I might have written songs.
Yeah, you wrote songs in the ‘80s.
What are your favorites, Amy?
Of that period?
Of that period. The ‘80s and ‘90s.
Gosh, I like all of them. Let me look at the list...
Well, “Was” is one you and your dad recorded together...
Yes, I recorded that. That’s a beautiful song. Then there’s a lot... Like, “Numbers On Paper” is a beautiful one. I’d have to look to see.
Georgie Fame did “Was.” He said the first time he heard it, it made him cry. Susan and Ralph... Mose’s cousin Susan married Ralph, who was his really best friend...
“Ever Since I Stole The Blues” is funny. “Ever Since the World Ended”...
Oh, it was about Ralph?
Well, it wasn’t about Ralph. It’s just that it was a line, “Susan and Ralph looking at old photographs...”

There are a lot of great songs that are not so well known. “Fires of Spring.” “Perfect Moment.” There are all these, like, “What Do You Do After You Ruin Your Life?” But I’m trying to think from the ‘80s... Like, “The Earth Wants You.” That was another one from my period.
Mmm-hmm.
You know “The Earth Wants You,” Dad. What was on that record? Oh, I might have it on my phone. I just realized.

Here’s the lyric in the book. It’s so beautiful. “When I become was / And we become Were / Will there be any sign or a trace / Of the lovely contour of your face / And will there be someone around / With essentially my kind of sound.” Wow.
It’s a really pretty song. It’s on that doc... That’s what they ended that NPR thing with.
